It's not as easy for actresses," Toto said. Fox News Digital reached out to Lilly for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Two UK siblings inherited a £2 million estate from their mother; years of disputes led to £142,000 in tax interest and their removal as executors
articles.summary: When Grace Baillie Key died in September 2022, her estate included a house valued at £2 million and a shareholding in a family care-home business that she
articles.body: When Grace Baillie Key died in September 2022, her estate included a house valued at £2 million and a shareholding in a family care-home business that she left equally to her two children. What followed was a prolonged disagreement between Laura Key and Richard Key over how her estate should be managed, with their deteriorating relationship making it increasingly difficult to settle matters. According to Bailii England and Wales High Court (Chancery Division) Decisions, the dispute reached the High Court, where a judge considered whether the siblings could continue as joint executors or whether an independent professional should take over. By the time of the hearing, interest on the unpaid inheritance tax had risen to about £142,000, adding to the financial consequences of an estate that had remained unsettled for years.Siblings inherited £2 million property and equal shares in family care-home businessGrace Baillie Key died aged 84 on 28 September 2022, leaving a will dated 11 November 2014. Her children, Laura and Richard, were named as joint executors and were the only beneficiaries. The principal assets included Ebury Lodge, a property in Westland Green, Little Hadham, Hertfordshire, with a probate valuation of £2 million, alongside their mother's interest in Ebury Court Residential Home Limited. Under the will, each sibling was to receive half of that shareholding. Personal belongings and a small life insurance policy also formed part of the estate.As reported by Bailii England and Wales High Court (Chancery Division) Decisions, draft accounts prepared by Richard's solicitors put the gross estate at approximately £2.28 million as of November 2024. After liabilities of about £366,750, the net figure stood at roughly £1.91 million. The inheritance tax due at the date of death was calculated at £556,388, before interest was added. By 5 November 2024, that interest had reached £67,040, taking the combined tax bill to more than £623,000. At the later court hearing, the judge was told that the interest alone had climbed to around £142,000, accruing at £117.81 a day.The figures were not entirely accepted by Laura, who questioned some of the expenses included in the accounts, particularly costs she believed related to Richard's personal occupation of the property. The judge observed that she had not clearly identified which entries she accepted or set out a fuller response to the figures.Siblings’ inheritance dispute began soon after their mother’s deathThe relationship between the siblings had already broken down by the time their mother died. Within little more than a week, Laura had instructed solicitors to contact Richard over allegations that he had excluded her from Ebury Lodge and removed their mother's belongings. The correspondence also sought assurances about the handling of the property and its contents. Richard did not respond to those letters, according to the judgment.They also disagreed over the funeral arrangements, including whether there should be a service or a direct cremation. A service eventually took place, although Laura did not attend. The disagreements continued into the administration of the estate, with both siblings seeking information and questioning the other's decisions.Laura wanted an independent administrator from October 2022. Richard initially proposed a firm of solicitors, and both siblings instructed the firm BRM to deal with probate. By September 2023, the solicitors had stopped acting after receiving conflicting instructions, with their correspondence indicating that the lack of clear agreement had contributed to the costs.The judge later described the wider dispute as one marked by mutual mistrust, with responsibility for the difficulties resting on both sides.Ebury Lodge sale, mortgage arrears and occupation disputeEbury Lodge became a central point of disagreement. A market appraisal from Savills in November 2022 put its value between £2.25 million and £2.5 million. The property went on the market in April 2023 with an asking price of £2.5 million, but viewings were limited and no offers followed.A formal valuation completed in July 2023 put the property at £2 million. The house continued to be marketed, but the revised price did not attract a buyer either. After further discussions, the asking price was reduced to £2 million in late 2023. The property remained on the market until May 2024 without an offer.Richard proposed renting the house to generate income towards the mortgage and running costs. Laura opposed the idea, pointing to the mortgage lender's position that the property could not be rented and that the mortgage needed to be repaid. The judge criticised Richard's persistence with the proposal despite the lender's restriction. He also found that Richard had no proper grounds for entering a caveat against the estate in August 2023 after Laura refused to agree to renting the property. The caveat prevented a grant of probate from being obtained while it remained in place.Mortgage arrears added another layer of pressure. Richard said he had paid £22,031 towards the arrears in October 2023. In March 2024, their father, Rodney Key, paid £330,000, leaving a further balance outstanding. Richard later said he paid the remaining amount, allowing the mortgage to be discharged. His evidence was that his own contributions towards the arrears and redemption totalled £64,137, as reported.Richard also moved into Ebury Lodge after it had stood empty for around three years. Laura objected to his occupation and argued that he should pay rent to the estate. The judge accepted that having someone live in the property could help protect and maintain it, potentially benefiting the estate, but made clear that this did not automatically entitle Richard to live there without financial adjustment.A court battle over who should administer the estateLaura's application, issued in July 2025, sought the removal of both siblings as executors and the appointment of an independent administrator. Her complaints included the delay in dealing with probate, Richard's occupation of the house, the caveat and disputes over documents and money. She also made allegations concerning company funds, signatures and access to an online health account. Richard denied the allegations, and the judge found that several had not been substantiated in the estate proceedings or belonged to separate litigation concerning the family business.Richard argued that the estate was manageable and that the siblings could continue as joint executors, with the court providing directions on the matters they could not resolve themselves. He also maintained that appointing a professional would create unnecessary expense. Laura, by contrast, said their relationship had deteriorated to the point where joint administration was no longer practical.According to the Business and Property courts of England and Wales, the financial cost of the litigation was already substantial. By the time of the judgment, Laura's legal costs stood at £170,000 and Richard's at £96,000, bringing their combined costs to £266,000. Those expenses sat alongside the inheritance tax and accumulating interest, as well as the costs associated with the property and the estate's other liabilities.The judge concluded that there was no realistic prospect of the siblings working together to finish the administration. Resolving the immediate questions about the house would not, in his view, remove the underlying hostility or prevent further disputes.Court appoints independent firm to resolve inheritance disputeThe court appointed Cripps Trust Corporation Limited to administer the estate independently. The proposed fees were estimated at £6,000 to £9,000 plus VAT for the work needed to obtain probate, followed by £20,000 to £25,000 plus VAT for the subsequent administration. Although that appointment would add professional costs, the judge considered it a more workable option than leaving the siblings in a position where they could not agree.The ruling did not determine every dispute surrounding Ebury Lodge. Because Laura and Richard would no longer remain in office as executors, the court did not need to make final decisions on the property's sale price or the amount Richard might owe for living there. The judge did, however, offer guidance for the independent administrator.An expert report dated June 2026 valued Ebury Lodge at £1.65 million, below its earlier £2 million probate valuation and the initial asking price. The expert also estimated monthly rental values ranging from £3,485 in September 2022 to £4,250 in September 2025. The administrator will be able to consider the relevant valuation evidence, the benefit to the estate of Richard's occupation and the expenses he properly incurred maintaining the property.You use AI every day. articles.title: France is learning the hard way what happens when the socialist bill comes due
articles.summary: Paris is burning as rioters torch Limoges town hall and break into Marseille city hall while Emmanuel Macron remains notably absent amid the chaos.
articles.body: "Is Paris Burning?" The title of that 1960s movie came from a message Adolf Hitler sent to his commanding general in Paris in August 1944. He wanted Paris to burn if he couldn’t keep it. Today, the call isn’t coming from the Führerbunker; it’s from inside the house. It’s not Nazis, but the French — and quasi-French — burning Paris and other French cities. The Louvre museum in Paris, home to the Mona Lisa, closed Monday "due to a student social movement." That’s one way to describe the utter chaos overtaking French cities. PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE In Limoges, rioters set fire to the town hall, destroying its iconic tower. In Marseille, they broke into city hall and vandalized the interior. In Paris, a video circulating online appeared to show young thugs shouting, "Wallah! Kill her!" and "Dirty whore!" [my translation] at a policewoman they chased and threw to the ground — all while trashing property and assaulting people on the streets. What’s happening in France is both familiar and new. It’s familiar in that mass protests are endemic to France. They happen every few years when a feckless government tries to balance the books by reforming France’s ruinously generous public benefits. What’s new is the addition of foreign influence and the scale of the violence. FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’ The high-schoolers who kicked off this round of protests are angry about class sizes, dilapidated schools, and access to college. Retirees who joined them say state pensions aren’t enough to live on. Everyone complains about the high cost of living. They all want more state spending to cure their ills. French protests often turn violent. Torched cars, vandalized property, and looting are common. What has added fuel to the fire this time is the "Casseurs" (breakers), looters, and violent thugs going beyond what was tacitly tolerated in the past. Towns have municipal police, but they aren’t equipped or trained for law enforcement, let alone riot control. France has specialized riot-control units, but only so many. articles.title: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says
articles.summary: The government is expected to accept all 27 recommendations made in the review by ex-Ofsted boss, Sir David Bell.
articles.body:
Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it following a major review, the BBC understands.

It means anti-Jewish hatred would be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.

The government-commissioned review into antisemitism in education is also expected to recommend dedicated training for teachers, more consistent recording and reporting of incidents, and better education about antisemitism and modern-day Jewish life.

The BBC understands it will also call for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

The review, led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell, is due to be presented to Parliament on Wednesday. The government is expected to accept all 27 recommendations.

It was launched amid growing concern about antisemitism in the UK, following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025 , in which two men were killed.

Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC

Antisemitic incident reports rise by a fifth in first half of 2026

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.

The review is also expected to recommend that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot."

Staff and pupils told the BBC they have become so used to these measures that they barely notice them anymore.

Lock-in - or "in-vacuation" - drills for dealing with intruders have become second nature, even to the youngest pupils.

"It's a bit scary sometimes, but you know you're safe," said Livi, a Year 6 pupil.

"It's sad that we can't be equal to everyone else, but people don't like us just because of the way we are," added her classmate, Sadie.

A group of a dozen older pupils who spoke to the BBC said that while they feel safe inside school, hearing about antisemitic attacks in the UK, including reports of pupils at other Jewish schools being harassed on their commute and at sports fixtures, has left them feeling targeted.

Some said that they were reluctant to wear skullcaps or necklaces featuring the Star of David – a Jewish symbol – outside school.

"Other religions get to be out and wear their necklaces and be proud - I don't get why Jewish people can't do it as much," said Year 9 pupil Ilan.

In response to the recommendations, the government is also expected to encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

He added: "We have advocated these measures be accompanied by other steps including improving education about Jewish life and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality."

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

The Department for Education has declined to comment before the review is published.

articles.title: A London bachelor died with a £2.7 million estate and no will in 2018; a High Court DNA battle over his father’s relationships decided who inherited the fortune
articles.summary: McDonald Noel, a wealthy London bachelor who died in 2018, aged nearly 84, left behind a £2.7 million estate without a will, spouse or children.
articles.body: McDonald Noel, a wealthy London bachelor who died in 2018, aged nearly 84, left behind a £2.7 million estate without a will, spouse or children. Years later, his fortune has become the subject of a High Court dispute over who qualifies as his rightful heir. The case centres on DNA evidence, family records and questions about the relationships of his father, Stanley Dorant, who fathered children in Trinidad and Barbados. Noel, who emigrated from Trinidad to London in 1960, was a shopkeeper and property tycoon.According to The Independent, Noel’s estate included a Kensington home valued at £1.5 million. Heir hunters identified potential relatives across the UK and Caribbean, but competing claims over their family connections have led to a High Court dispute over who should inherit his £2.7 million fortune.McDonald Noel's £2.7 million estate becomes the subject of a High Court disputeMcDonald Noel died in London in April 2018, leaving a gross estate valued at £2.7 million. The estate included a Kensington property worth £1.5 million. Noel was born in Trinidad in 1934 and moved to London in 1960. He died at the age of nearly 84 without a spouse, children or a will. His death left the question of inheritance unresolved.Without eligible relatives, his fortune was destined for government coffers. However, heir hunters from a firm called Hoopers began investigating his family tree to identify potential beneficiaries in the UK and Caribbean. Their investigation uncovered competing claims from several branches of his extended family, prompting a High Court inquiry into his ancestry and the evidence supporting each claimant's relationship to Noel.Stanley Dorant’s family relationships become central to the £2.7 million inheritance battleStanley Dorant, Noel's father, was born in Barbados in 1906 and died in Trinidad in 1968. Noel's mother, Neutrice Dorant, had another child, Stella, in 1933, before Noel's birth the following year. Neutrice died in 1938. Stanley later married Clementina Forde in 1939 after she joined him in Trinidad.Clementina already had two sons, Clyde and St Clair, while Stanley and Clementina also had a son, Francis. Descendants of these family members disagree over whether Stanley fathered all the children attributed to him. Documentary records show that Stanley travelled between Trinidad and Barbados and fathered children on both islands.DNA evidence and family records support competing claims to Noel's fortuneThe claimants include Gerard Burton, Stella's son, who argues that his mother was Stanley's daughter and therefore Noel's full sister. He could potentially receive the entire estate if the court accepts that claim. Francis's son, Shaka, is also seeking a share. Desiree Dorant, representing St Clair's children, and Tyler Dorant, representing Clyde's grandchildren, maintain that their branches are descended from Stanley and should inherit.Lawyers presented DNA results, historical records, and witness evidence to support their respective positions. Daniel Burton, representing Desiree and her siblings, argued that the evidence supported Stanley's paternity of Clyde and St Clair. He cited historical travel records and DNA evidence in support of their claims to the estate.Lawyers disagree over whether Stanley fathered all the children named in the caseAidan Briggs, representing Shaka, urged the judge to approach the claims differently. He argued that Stanley was named as the father on only two birth certificates, those of Noel and Francis. He also cautioned against treating family beliefs or Stanley's role in the children's lives as proof of biological paternity.Briggs said the DNA evidence supported the claims of Stella and Francis but challenged those of Clyde and St Clair. He argued that the court must be satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that Stanley fathered the other children. Master Katherine McQuail heard the case as part of a rare legal kin enquiry.Who inherited McDonald Noel’s £2.7 million estate after the High Court rulingAccording to the UK National Archives, the dispute has since been resolved. In a judgment handed down on 23 December 2025, Master McQuail found that Stanley Dorant’s biological children were McDonald Noel, St Clair and Francis only. The court was not satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that Stanley fathered Clyde or Stella. For Stella, the judge noted that Stanley’s name was absent from her birth certificate and that the DNA evidence was only weakly supportive.For Clyde, there was no evidence that Stanley was in Barbados when Clyde was conceived, and no DNA sample was provided by any of his descendants. As a result, Gerard Burton did not inherit the whole estate and Tyler Dorant’s claim failed. The court directed that the estate be distributed among the issue of McDonald’s half-siblings: Shaka Dorant, as Francis’s son, and Desiree Dorant and her siblings, as St Clair’s children.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jane Doe says embattled Cornell head Kotlikoff doubted her gang-rape claim
articles.summary: As a no-confidence vote looms, Cornell says the characterisation of the head's reaction is "incorrect".
articles.body:
A former Cornell student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has said she felt "unsupported and disbelieved" by the university president.

Known anonymously as Jane Doe, she has written a letter accusing President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York says her account of the Cornell head's reaction is "incorrect".

She addressed her letter to campus faculty who will hold a rare vote this month on Kotlikoff's leadership. Doe filed her lawsuit last month alleging she was raped by several men in October 2024 at a Chi Phi fraternity party.

All seven former fraternity members accused by Doe have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police, and the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but the case has since reopened .

Responding to Doe's initial allegation, Cornell said it had opened an internal investigation, as well as a civil rights inquiry.

What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation

In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a second-hand account" of Kotlikoff's reaction and that his "initial response" was "along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'"

Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party.

She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom "appeared distressed" by the college president's question.

Doe said in her letter: "It diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."

She said she wrote the letter so that faculty "can make an informed choice" ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff's leadership.

The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe's lawyer.

But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: "The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account."

The spokesperson said Kotlikoff's question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape "was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024".

"He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting," the spokesperson said.

Kotlikoff, who has led the Ithaca-based institution for 26 years, was grilled by the faculty senate last Wednesday.

Staff said they were "deeply disturbed" by his handling of the case and accused him of lacking an "emotional response", according to recordings obtained by the BBC.

Kotlikoff highlighted changes the university had introduced as a result of Doe's allegations, including banning fraternity parties.

"We are all extraordinarily upset by the events at Cornell in October of 2024," he said.

The faculty senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff at Cornell, scheduled their no-confidence vote for 28 October.

In recordings of the meeting, faculty said sexual misconduct on campus was a systemic problem that demanded "systemic attention".

Paul Ortiz, a labour history professor who sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said students had told faculty they "feel unsafe walking to the library after dark".

He accused Cornell of treating rape "as more of a 'PR problem' than a heinous crime".

Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults

articles.title: That bacon on your plate may have just been recalled — here’s what you need to know to stay safe
articles.summary: More than 1.5 million pounds of meat was just recalled after possibly being stored unsafely — here’s what you should know if you have the affected products.
articles.body: Don’t fire that breakfast griddle up just yet — your bacon may be at risk. On October 17, Kayem Foods Inc. issued a recall for more than 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat products that may have been stored at improper temperatures, according to an announcement from the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS). This includes bacon, deli meats, poultry and more, with an extensive list of potentially affected products that may be sitting in your fridge right now. Keep reading to find out more about which products were affected, and what to do if you have them. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is included in the Kayem Foods meat recall? Kayem Foods, Inc. has recalled several meats because they may have experienced temperature abuse while being stored prior to delivery. The issue was found after a retail customer complained of warm product temperatures on October 1, after which an investigation was conducted. The investigation determined that a range of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products were being stored in a warehouse cooler with inconsistencies in temperature that make them potentially unsafe to consume. Cold food should be kept at or below 40 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the FSIS — anything above that can result in spoilage and bacteria growth, potentially causing food poisoning or other illness. Inside the USDA inspection seal, the recalled products have establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” and “EST. M 9520”. The products were produced approximately between March 31 and Oct. 7 and shipped to retailers nationwide and in Hong Kong. The list includes hot dogs, bacon, turkey breast (deli meat), corned beef, chicken sausage and more — you can check here for a full list of recalled products and check to see if you have any (there’s also an abbreviated list with images). Consumers can also contact Kayem Foods’ customer service Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET at 800-426-6100 or email them at info@kayem.com. What to do if you have the recalled meat? If your meat was recalled, you should throw it out. Alternatively, the FSIS recommends returning it to your place of purchase, but above all, it stresses that consumers should not consume the meat. Even when cooked to a proper temperature, there’s no way to guarantee the meat’s safety, and you can’t tell just by looking at it, either. “One of the most important things for consumers to understand is that you cannot reliably determine whether food is safe by looking at it, smelling it, or tasting it,” Melissa Vaccaro, senior food safety program specialist at the National Environmental Health Association, told NBC Selected in our guide to food safety during a power outage. “Food can contain disease-causing microorganisms without looking or smelling spoiled. And never taste questionable food to decide whether it is safe.” The best products for keeping your meat safe There are products that can help you keep your meat temperature-safe during storage and preparation. Remember that these aren’t solutions to official recall warnings, and all contaminated products should be thrown away or returned — not consumed. The products below, however, can help you store non-recalled food and ensure that your method of storing keeps it safe to eat. Digital thermometers can alert you to temperature changes in your fridge or freezer that can result in spoiled food. This thermometer includes one fridge and one freezer thermometer, each of which sends real-time readings to the LCD display, according to the brand. The LCD display has a magnetic backing for mounting to the front of a fridge, and a foldout stand for countertop placement, and includes a programmable alarm as well. This can be especially helpful to alert you of the temperature drop if the power goes out overnight, giving you the opportunity to move your food to a cooler or insulated bag. Insulated grocery bags are great for keeping your food cold or frozen on your way back from the store, and these lightweight bags can keep food cold or hot for up to an hour and a half, according to the brand. They’re also foldable, making them easy to store, and can hold up to 25 pounds of groceries in each bag. You can use these ice packs to keep food and other contents cold for up to 48 hours, according to Cooler Shock. Once you add water and freeze them, the nylon exterior holds up over time, so you won’t need to restock the ice again. It’s great for coolers and totes, and comes in packs of three or five in varying sizes. These are ideal if you’re heading to the beach or pool and want to bring sandwiches, hot dogs or other food that needs to be kept at a certain temperature for safe consumption. While cooking recalled meat will not make it safe to eat, a meat thermometer is handy for ensuring that non-recalled meat and poultry is cooked to a safe temperature. This one lets you read temperatures in either Fahrenheit or Celsius, and has an LCD screen with large numbers, making it easy to read, according to the brand. It also includes a storage sleeve for safekeeping, which has a protein temperature chart on the side for reference while cooking. Why trust NBC Selected? I am an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected who’s been covering various topics for more than two years. I frequently report on skin care news, along with weekly reporting on sales and deals from prominent brands and retailers. For this piece, I researched the recall on Kayem Foods Inc. meat products to find out everything you need to know about its recent recall. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: In 2021, an 88-acre former limestone quarry in Indiana became a reservoir holding 3.2 billion gallons of water to protect supplies during droughts
articles.summary: In Fishers, Indiana, an 88-acre abandoned limestone quarry has been transformed into a reservoir capable of holding 3.5 billion gallons of water, serving as a vital buffer against droughts and helping meet the rising water demand in Central Indiana.
articles.body: A retired limestone quarry was converted into a reservoir in Fishers, Indiana, near Geist Reservoir in 2021, to act as an additional buffer against drought and meet the rising demand across Central Indiana. According to Schnabel Engineering, the facility provides water storage of 3.2 billion gallons and can hold roughly half the volume of neighbouring Geist Reservoir, despite occupying less than one-twentieth of its surface area. Central Indiana was projected to require an additional 50 million gallons of water per day by 2050, making additional storage an important part of preparing for future demand.Why Central Indiana required additional water storage As per the Environmental Resilience Institute, the Indianapolis region receives about 42 inches of rainfall annually, but the timing is unpredictable. The region has to navigate the problem of heavy rainfall that exceeds storage capacity and, conversely, dry spells, which strain the water supply. During the 2012 drought, the severity of this problem became apparent when Geist Reservoir fell 18 inches, while Eagle Creek Reservoir dropped a foot, as per the Indianapolis Business Journal. Moreover, restrictions were imposed on water supply in communities as a sustainable measure during the dry conditions.The event served as a stark reminder of how water can be affected under extreme weather, and this vulnerability was further aggravated by population and economic activity. Citizens Energy Group began preliminary planning for the new facility in 2013. During the feasibility stage, engineers examined whether the abandoned quarry's limestone walls could contain stored water over extended periods. The utility also worked with the City of Fishers to assess planning requirements, construction impacts, and potential conflicts with future development.How an abandoned quarry became a water reserve Rather than simply filling the excavation, the intake and pumping systems had to go underground. According to Schnabel Engineering, there were four 220-foot-deep, 60-inch excavated-diameter well shafts, alongside a separate tunnel approximately 250 feet long. Drill and blast methods were used to construct the intake shafts and tunnels, while slope stabilisation was used around the quarry walls and rim, and a dedicated access road and perimeter fencing were added.The reservoir's operating principle is quite straightforward: if Geist Reservoir receives more water than its storage capacity, an intake structure diverts some of the excess into the quarry. Whereas when supplies are needed, the water stored is returned by a pump station to Geist Reservoir, from which it goes directly into the downstream system serving the region. As per the Indianapolis Business Journal, the intake could divert up to 100 million US gallons daily, while the pumping system could return up to 30 million gallons. These are maximum transfer rates, distinct from the reservoir's overall storage capacity.As per the Environmental Resilience Institute, the cost of the land was $13 million and construction added another $17 million. This brought the total amount to $30 million, which was financed through Citizens Energy Group's capital budget. To put savings in perspective, the university’s case study estimates that constructing a conventional reservoir of comparable capacity would have cost between $600 million and $700 million. So, reusing the quarry was a more feasible alternative; however, these initial figures do not represent an exhaustive comparison of every possible reservoir design.You use AI every day. articles.title: Draft law to deal with Troubles legacy backed by MPs
articles.summary: MPs voted 330 to 178 in favour of the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Legislation aimed at tackling the legacy of the Troubles in Northern Ireland has passed its stages in the House of Commons.

The long-awaited bill was backed by 330 MPs with 178 voting against following two days of intensive debate over the details of hundreds of amendments.

It will now proceed to the House of Lords to face further scrutiny, which is expected to continue into next year.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant described the bill as being about "honesty, candour, the pursuit of justice and most importantly truth".

He said "although much of the debate has been about veterans" the planned legislation was "actually primarily about families".

The bill seeks to address the unresolved legacy of decades-long violent conflict known as the Troubles in which thousands of people were killed.

It was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government .

The bill would replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act, which banned inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents.

The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful.

Labour's plan involves a legacy commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

Last week the government published a series of amendments, including a requirement for the attorney general to provide consent for any serious prosecutions.

The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.

But the secretary of state rejected claims the changes amounted to an "amnesty" for former soldiers.

While some have argued protections for veterans do not go far enough, Sinn Féin has branded the amendments a "veterans' charter".

The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has also raised concerns that MPs have not been given enough time to scrutinise the changes.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, Sir Chris said the bill was seeking to achieve a "balance" in its provisions.

"This bill isn't about one group or another," he told MPs towards the conclusion of several hours of debate.

"It's not about special favours for one group or another."

A spokesperson for the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs said the amendments on the bill marked an "important milestone".

"Last year's joint framework was a momentous step forward, and what is needed now is full and timely implementation," they said.

The Foreign Affairs Minister, Helen McEntee, had been in close contact with the NI secretary over the past number of weeks, the statement continued.

"It is vital that implementing legislation is compliant with the ECHR [European Court of Human Rights] and faithful to the joint framework, so that it can deliver for victims and their families.

articles.title: A Florida developer floated 864 apartments near Sarasota’s Celery Fields, then offered a 126-home settlement on the same 51 acres; county commissioners rejected the deal and voted to explore buying the land instead
articles.summary: Sarasota County officials have rejected a proposed settlement that would have permitted a 126-home subdivision beside the Celery Fields, opting instead to
articles.body: Sarasota County officials have rejected a proposed settlement that would have permitted a 126-home subdivision beside the Celery Fields, opting instead to explore purchasing the disputed property for conservation and stormwater management. The decision, reported by Sarasota Magazine on October 8, 2026, follows a prolonged legal battle involving homebuilder D.R. Horton, the property owners and the county over development rights on approximately 51 acres along Raymond Road. The move leaves the litigation unresolved but opens the possibility of protecting the land through public ownership rather than residential construction.County considers acquisition after rejecting settlementAt an October 6 meeting, county commissioners voted unanimously against the settlement and separately directed county administration and the county attorney’s office to negotiate with D.R. Horton and the Smith Farm property owners over a potential purchase.The decision does not commit the county to buying the property. Officials have yet to establish a purchase price, identify funding or set a timetable for negotiations. Any acquisition would depend on the parties agreeing to acceptable terms.Commissioners stressed that the property’s value extends beyond its development potential. Located next to the Celery Fields, the land could contribute to stormwater management while helping preserve habitat in an area known for its birdlife and outdoor recreation. Commissioner Teresa Mast backed exploring an acquisition, while Commissioner Mark Smith emphasised the need for a realistic appraisal to ensure the county pays a fair price.From 126 homes to a proposal for 864 apartmentsThe dispute dates back to D.R. Horton’s plans to build a single-family subdivision on the property. The homebuilder initially proposed approximately 170 homes before reducing the plan to 126. County commissioners rejected the revised proposal in February 2025, prompting the developer and property owners to challenge the rezoning decision in court.A separate development proposal subsequently raised the stakes. The parties pursued a plan for 864 apartments in buildings up to 65 feet tall under Florida’s Live Local Act, which is designed to encourage affordable housing development. Whether the property’s Open Use Rural zoning makes it eligible for that proposal has become part of the legal dispute.The latest settlement would have resolved the pending litigation by allowing the 126-home subdivision to proceed. Commissioners declined that option, choosing to investigate whether purchasing the land could offer a longer-term alternative.Sarasota Audubon offers fundraising supportSarasota Audubon Society has backed the county’s efforts to protect the property, citing its potential contribution to wildlife conservation and flood management. During public comment, the organisation’s president, Sara Reisinger, urged commissioners to acquire the land and integrate it into the Celery Fields’ stormwater system. She also said the society had spent nearly $20,000 supporting the county’s position in the rezoning and Live Local Act disputes.Reisinger offered to help raise additional money if needed to close a funding gap in a potential purchase, opening the door to a public-private partnership. However, commissioners have not established how much additional stormwater capacity an acquisition would provide, nor have they determined the financial terms required to secure the land.What happens next?The county will now explore a fair-market purchase with the developer and property owners. County Attorney Joshua Moye told commissioners that buying the property had been discussed during an earlier dispute-resolution process, but D.R. Horton had rejected the idea at that time. No fresh acquisition negotiations had taken place in response to the latest settlement offer.For now, the future of the 51-acre property remains uncertain. articles.title: Kyle Kennedy, granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, dies at 42
articles.summary: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury.
articles.body: Kyle Francis Kennedy, an educator and granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, died last month after suffering a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis and years of medical issues, a Massachusetts funeral home said. She was 42. Kennedy “passed away peacefully” on Sept. 21 at her home in Westwood, Massachusetts, according to an obituary by Burke Funeral Homes. Her cause of death was not announced. She “built a career devoted to early childhood education,” the obituary said. “Blessed with a formidable intellect, dry wit, and beauty, she will be remembered for her devotion to her children Conor, Josephine, and Declan, and her support for educational reform for disadvantaged children and for people living with disabilities.” Kennedy grew up in Cohasset, Massachusetts, and attended the prestigious Milton Academy before matriculating to Georgetown University. She spent a semester abroad in Florence, Italy, which “left a lasting mark” and led to her “deep love of Tuscan Renaissance art and a lifelong talent for making pasta dishes from scratch,” the obituary said. She earned a master’s degree in early education from Pace University and another master’s in education policy from Harvard. Kennedy spent two years in the Teach for America program, working in the New York City public school system in “an experience that launched a career in education,” according to her obituary. “She went on to become a passionate advocate for more equitable elementary education and charter schooling, later working with technology companies focused on reforming and improving school curricula, and as a coach for educators working with young students,” the obituary said. Kennedy was the daughter of Michael LeMoyne Kennedy, the sixth child of RFK and Ethel Kennedy. Michael LeMoyne Kennedy was just 39 when he was fatally injured on Dec. 31, 1997, in Colorado, slamming into a tree while playing ski-football on an icy Aspen slope. Like many in her famed family, Kyle Kennedy was fond of the outdoors and sports. She ran in the 2019 Boston Marathon, competing under her married name, Kyle Kerr. But she spent the last several years of life unable to walk. “In 2020, Kyle suffered a severe spinal cord injury that resulted in long term paralysis, disability, and other medical challenges,” the obituary said. “The years that followed brought struggles but Kyle fought to maintain her dry wit and determination through it all, trying to be the best possible mother to her sons and caring for her two beloved, ill-behaved Wheaten terriers.” It was not disclosed how Kennedy suffered that traumatic 2020 injury. “She also began to advocate for people living with disabilities, including testifying at the Massachusetts state house in a hearing on discrimination in disabled health care,” the funeral home added. Kennedy is survived by her sons, Conor, 12, and Declan, 10; her ex-husband, Liam Kerr; her mother, Victoria Denise Gifford; her brother, Michael LeMoyne Kennedy Jr.; and her sister, Rory Gifford Kennedy.

articles.title: NFL clears Philadelphia Eagles of wrongdoing in handling of Jalen Hurts blood clot situation
articles.summary: The NFL closed its review of how the Philadelphia Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clot situation ahead of the London Jaguars game.
articles.body: The NFL is satisfied with the manner in which the Philadelphia Eagles handled the Jalen Hurts blood clot situation the past two weeks, a league source confirmed on Tuesday. The matter is closed as far as the league is concerned. That means the NFL review of the matter will not result in any team punishment for how the Eagles handled the injury designation for Hurts ahead of the Week 5 game between them and the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. EAGLES QUARTERBACK JALEN HURTS RULED OUT OF SUNDAY'S GAME 'OUT OF AN ABUNDANCE OF CAUTION' DUE TO BLOOD CLOT The Eagles did not report Hurts had been discovered to have a superficial blood clot the day before the game. Hurts played in the game and even practiced multiple days afterward. But late last week further evaluations revealed that Hurts has a deep vein trombosis as well as a bilateral pulmonary emboli – which the Eagles and Hurts' agent announced on Monday. Hurts is out for the remainder of the season. The Eagles have made it clear they have been in contact with the league throughout the process. That process included the NFL's chief medical doctor having Hurts seen at the Cleveland Clinic in London on that fateful Saturday before the game against Jacksonville. The NFL released a statement provided to OutKick and Fox News Digital on the matter: "The league had been in contact throughout the process with the Eagles medical personnel, and the Cleveland Clinic in London where the tests were conducted. "The league’s Chief Medical Officer Dr. Allen Sills arranges for medical resources with leading providers in every international market with approval from the NFL Players Association. "Medical care for players is provided by club medical staff in coordination with independent doctors." After the superficial blood clot in Hurts’ calf was first discovered, the team, staff, doctors and Hurts made the determination that he could play the following day against the Jaguars. Aside from their two publicly disseminated statements on the matter, the only person in the Eagles organization to discuss the Hurts matter is coach Nick Sirianni. And he hasn't been forthcoming. "You know, the health of our players are, is always at the forefront of our mind," Sirianni said. "And leave that up to the medical experts, but we always, always care deeply about our players. And that's when you are completely focused on together and connection. You're always thinking about the well-being of your guys and that's what we were in that situation." Beyond that, Sirianni repeated during his press conference on Monday that he is not a medical expert and added, "I trust the people that are involved in helping us all make these decisions." But the club had no one from the medical staff answer reporters' questions. GM Howie Roseman, who is in charge of the medical staff under the Eagles structure, also did not address the matter. Roseman typically does not speak with reporters during the season, in deference to the coaching staff's messaging, with the rare exception of trades being made and an NFL-required availability. The lack of answers from the team has opened the door to more questions. And those will persist even as the team and the league are trying to move forward. articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: France braces for more unrest after parts of Paris spun out of control
articles.summary: French Prime Minister Lecornu says a massive police operation backed by the military will counter the next protest set for this weekend in France.
articles.body: PARIS, France: Paris is burning. Yet again. But this time, according to officials and analysts, it’s different. And unrest here could have a lasting impact on France… perhaps the world. I have been covering protests in France for decades. I lived in Paris for nine years. I know that the French are very skilled at taking politics to the street. The recent upheaval has many worried. From all the people I hear from on the ground here, the rioting has been more violent, more destructive, more profound. Domestic strife seemingly out of control. FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS When I approached the bar at a brasserie near Place de la Republique, the server asked if I was an American and a journalist. After replying yes to both he concluded, "So you’ve come to cover the civil war." The numbers tell the tale. Some 2,500 arrests during the last weekend of clashes between protesters and police. Around 1,000 officers injured. Many hurt, some seriously, on the activists’ side. And about 3,000 businesses impacted, trashed, looted. Damage estimated over one billion dollars. FRANCE'S MASSIVE INTEL FAILURE SPARKS RESIGNATION OFFERS AMID DAYS OF RIOTING What was most striking were the attacks on official buildings. An historic city hall in Limoges. A police headquarters in crime-ridden Marseille. An important tourist office in Lyon. Symbols of a French government under siege. The mostly peaceful protests supporting recent student concerns, as well as working and middle-class economic worries, hijacked by those bent on anarchy. And opportunistic young crooks looking for cheap thrills. Yes, there are immigrants and foreigners amid the rabble. Plus, those said to have ties with so-called "ultra-left" groupings. But this remains a very French uprising. Which in a way makes it even more unsettling. Nearly ten years of rule by President Emmanuel Macron has left this country more divided, with promises unfilled, anger near the surface. And violence a real danger. FRENCH NEWSPAPER RIPS MACRON AFTER RIOTS ERUPT ACROSS FRANCE: ‘INDELIBLE STAIN’ What was also deeply troubling about the latest bout of violence — and authorities have admitted it — is that there were periods of time when parts of Paris and other cities were out of control. Shop owners were forced to fend for themselves. All of this plum pickings for politicians on the left and right. Either sympathizing with protesters’ demands. Or calling for more law and order. Both sides slamming those in power. With presidential elections upcoming in six months, timing is everything. With the French treasury bare, it seems the more pressing and more promising route for the current authorities is greater security. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That’s why top government officials have been speaking out about their planning for the next big protest set for this weekend. French Prime Minister Lecornu says it will be countered by a "massive police operation" backed by the military. Activists will have to choose, Lecornu went on to say, between "violence" and the French "republic." "Do or die" talk that still does not address the underlying problems, not just facing France but other countries as well. That’s why, in addition to the curiosity factor of everyone being intrigued by France, it could also provide some real-time lessons on how or how not to deal with a brave new world of inequality and dwindling resources. See you at the "barricades."

articles.title: Court-martialled Army man among three held for killing cousin’s wife in land row in Gurgaon
articles.summary: Three arrested in Gurgaon’s Daulah village for Neetu’s murder over a land dispute; court-martialled ex-Army man Sandeep named mastermind, say police.
articles.body: Gurgaon: Three men, including the alleged mastermind, have been arrested for the murder of a 34-year-old woman whose body was found with her hands tied and mouth taped at her home in Daulah village in Sohna on Oct 16. Police said a dispute over a land deal prompted the woman’s husband’s paternal cousin, Sandeep, to allegedly plot the murder with the help of two associates.The deceased, Neetu, was found dead by her husband, Prashant, a private school teacher, when he returned home with their children in the afternoon. He found household belongings scattered around the house and Neetu lying in the bathroom. He removed the tape, untied her hands and rushed her to a hospital, where doctors declared her dead.Police identified the accused as Sandeep (35), a resident of Daulah, Anuj Rana (29) and Avnish (30), both residents of Roorkee in Uttarakhand’s Haridwar district.According to police, Sandeep held a grudge against Neetu after she persuaded her husband to return Rs 1 lakh that Sandeep had paid as an advance for purchasing their land. Investigators said Sandeep wanted to facilitate the sale of the seven-kanal (0.8-acre) plot, but Neetu considered the agreed price too low and convinced her husband to return the money. Police said this led Sandeep to plan her murder.The alleged conspiracy had been in the making for nearly two months, police said, adding that the accused conducted reconnaissance of Neetu’s house on Aug 31.According to ACP Naveen Sharma, Anuj and Avnish travelled from Roorkee to Daulah on the morning of the crime. Sandeep, accompanied by the two men, reached Neetu’s house around 9am, but they returned without executing the plan after finding her talking on the phone.Around 10.05am, Sandeep and Anuj allegedly entered the house while Avnish remained outside to keep watch. Police said they had brought tape and rope in a bag carried by Sandeep. The two men allegedly taped Neetu’s mouth, tied her hands with rope and strangled her.Neetu’s husband had left home around 7.45am. When he returned in the afternoon, he discovered the murder and rushed her to hospital.The killing triggered anger in the village. On Oct 17, residents blocked the busy Sohna-Gurgaon road for about an hour, demanding the immediate arrest of those responsible.Teams from crime branch Sohna, led by SI Rajesh, and crime branch Manesar, led by SI Sumit, arrested Sandeep in Sohna on Oct 19. Anuj Rana and Avnish were arrested in Roorkee on Oct 20, police said.Investigators said Sandeep had earlier served in the Indian Army but was court-martialled and dismissed in 2023 over his alleged involvement in extorting money on the pretext of securing jobs and other fraudulent activities. Police said he continued to be involved in alleged fraud after leaving the Army.“Sandeep planned to kill Neetu over seven kanals of land. He knew Anuj because the latter worked as a contract-based cook in the Army. Anuj works with the electricity department in his home state on a contract basis, while Avnish is a delivery executive and also works as a milkman,” ACP Sharma said. Sandeep had allegedly promised Rs 10 lakh to his accomplices.A police officer said Sandeep did not flee after the murder and was also present at Neetu’s cremation. “The three accused were captured on CCTV, and the family had suspected Sandeep’s involvement because of frequent arguments over the property. We eventually apprehended Sandeep, following which he revealed the identities of his co-accused,” the officer added.Police said the accused also took gold and silver jewellery from the house. The motorcycle allegedly used in the crime belonged to Anuj, police said.Sandeep was produced before a court on Oct 19 and remanded to four days of police custody. He is being questioned as part of the ongoing investigation.An FIR has been registered at Sohna Sadar police station under sections 103(1) (murder), 127(2) (wrongful restraint), 332(a) (dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property) and 3(5) (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of BNS.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: ‘Specific case, not blanket consent’: Punjab on handing over Jhota murder to CBI
articles.summary: Punjab says handing Jhota murder probe to CBI is case-specific, not blanket consent, while challenging HC-ordered CBI corruption probe of CM Mann’s OSD.
articles.body: ‘Chandigarh: Punjab govt on Tuesday justified its decision to hand over anti-drug activist Parminder Singh Jhota’s murder probe to the CBI while simultaneously fighting in court against the agency’s corruption probe linked to CM Bhagwant Mann’s OSD Rajbir Ghuman and five others.Responding to queries about the state govt challenging the high court order handing over the corruption probe against CM Mann’s OSD Rajbir Ghuman to CBI, while itself referring Jhota’s murder to the central agency, finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema said: “The previous Congress govt had revoked the CBI’s general jurisdiction in Punjab. The case (against CM’s OSD) was an instance of ‘political targeting by the BJP,’ which we will fight in courts and among people. In contrast, referring the activist’s killing to the CBI was an ‘administrative’ decision.”Asked if the Punjab govt was now in a way reviving the CBI’s jurisdiction in the state, Cheema said, “No, the probe has been referred to the CBI as a specific single case. This decision has been taken after due consultation with the state’s legal team about the issue of CBI’s barred jurisdiction.”In the petition filed before Supreme Court challenging high court’s order for a CBI investigation into the case linked to the CM’s OSD, the Punjab govt had contended that the CBI has no general (blanket) jurisdiction in Punjab. The state govt argued that since general consent was revoked in Nov 2020, the central agency cannot directly register FIRs or initiate probes without specific state permission or adherence to mandatory statutory protections.It was the previous Congress govt that had withdrawn the general consent granted to the CBI to investigate cases in the state, effectively requiring the CBI to take permission from the state govt on a case-to-case basis.Under Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, the CBI needs “general consent” from a state govt to operate and investigate cases freely within that state. Many opposition-ruled states—including Punjab, under a previous govt—withdrew this blanket consent years ago to block direct, unvetted CBI entry.The CBI registered an FIR against Ghuman and five others on the directions of the high court to investigate corruption allegations. In its plea to the apex court, the state govt argued that high court’s directive bypassed mandatory legal protections. articles.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
articles.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
articles.body:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.

Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"

But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?

Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.

Just listen to the way they talk about each other.

"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.

The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.

Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.

But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."

Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.

"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.

But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?

After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.

The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.

One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.

Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.

Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.

Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.

Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.

Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.

Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.

"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.

Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".

For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.

Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.

Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.

"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.

On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.

The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.

Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink .

A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.

Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.

It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.

Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."

But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.

Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.

A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.

When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.

During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.

At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.

Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.

Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.

Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."

"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.

Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.

"I think we will have good results too," he said.

Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

articles.title: UK police re-arrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence
articles.summary: Duo was first arrested for suspected link to incident at US-run airbase used for striking Iran during this year’s war.
articles.body:
Police in the United Kingdom have re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service after an incident at a United States-run airbase in England last month.

Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.

One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27, when the suspected plot against RAF Fairford took place. The airbase in Gloucestershire in western England has been used to launch strikes on Iran during this year’s war.

The second suspect was first arrested on October 1. Until Tuesday, the men had been released on bail pending more investigation.

Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said the investigation was “hugely complex” and that detectives were looking at “many lines of enquiry”.

“This is very much a live investigation,” Taylor said in a statement, adding: “We consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.”

“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added.

British police declared a major incident in the area around RAF Fairford after a member of the public reported seeing three “suspicious” vans driving near the base.

Residents were forced to leave their homes as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.

Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives.

The incident prompted the US to pull its bombers out of RAF Fairford, while British authorities blamed Iran.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Ken McCallum, the UK’s domestic intelligence spy chief, warned that Iran and Russia were expanding attacks against military bases in the UK, adding that the RAF Fairford incident was not unique.

In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged.

articles.title: A couple bought a Chelsea property for £9.75 million, demolished and rebuilt it, then sold it for £27.15 million; a tax tribunal rejected HMRC’s argument that the project was a trading venture
articles.summary: A couple who bought a Chelsea property for £9.75 million, demolished the existing building and constructed a new house before selling it for £27.15
articles.body: A couple who bought a Chelsea property for £9.75 million, demolished the existing building and constructed a new house before selling it for £27.15 million have won a tax tribunal appeal against HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). Raymond and Diana Eyre faced a dispute over whether their redevelopment of the Burnsall Street property constituted a trading venture or the sale of a private residence. HMRC argued the property was acquired to make a profit, while the couple maintained that they intended to live there. In April 2025, the First-tier Tribunal ruled that the project was not a trading venture.Why did the tribunal reject HMRC’s trading argument over the Chelsea propertyHMRC’s position was that the Eyres had acquired Burnsall Street to redevelop and sell it for a profit. The tribunal recorded the tax authority’s argument that the property was “never an asset which the Appellants wished to hold and was rather acquired to be resold”. HMRC also relied on the development agreement with property developer, Finchatton, the arrangements for the marketing of the completed property and the circumstances surrounding its eventual sale.According to the First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber), the Eyres disputed that interpretation, arguing that they had originally intended to move into Burnsall Street as their home and sell their existing property in Holland Park. The tribunal examined contemporary documents, including correspondence with their bank, as well as evidence about their involvement in the design and construction of the Chelsea house. It concluded that the couple’s intention at the time they acquired the property was central to deciding whether the transaction amounted to trading. The judgment stated that the question was whether the intention to trade “existed at the time of the acquisition of the asset”.How did the Eyres’ plans to live in Chelsea influence the tax rulingThe tribunal found that the Eyres intended to move into Burnsall Street after refurbishing it and to sell their Holland Park property. Evidence included a note from their bank in May 2010 recording their intention to trade down from the Holland Park house and put it on the market after the anticipated works at Burnsall Street. The tribunal also considered the couple’s extensive involvement in the design and fitting out of the new property.The completed house included features tailored to the family’s requirements, such as a swimming pool, gym, wine cellar and bespoke living spaces. The Eyres also selected materials and equipment according to their personal preferences. The tribunal noted that some of these choices increased costs without necessarily improving the property’s saleability. It found that the couple’s involvement and the personal nature of the finished house were inconsistent with HMRC’s argument that they had acquired the property solely to make a profit on resale. The tribunal therefore concluded that the purchase, redevelopment and sale of Burnsall Street did not constitute a trading venture.How did the £27.15 million Chelsea sale affect the Eyres’ tax appealThe tribunal recorded that the Eyres exchanged contracts to sell Burnsall Street in November 2014 for £27.15 million, with a further £600,000 paid for the furniture. Completion took place on 2 February 2015. The judgment stated that, after costs, the Eyres’ share was approximately £8.5 million between them, while Finchatton received approximately £2.9 million. The tribunal also noted that the sale price was considerably higher than the parties had anticipated when the project began.The tribunal separately considered whether Burnsall Street qualified as the couple’s principal private residence for capital gains tax purposes. It found that they had occupied the property as their residence from July 2013 until they moved out around the beginning of February 2015, and that their nomination of Burnsall Street as their main residence entitled them to principal private residence relief for the relevant period. The judgment concluded that the appeals should be allowed on both the trading-venture issue and the principal-residence issue. However, the tribunal did not determine the final amount of tax payable, leaving that question for the parties to resolve in light of a separate judgment concerning the treatment of gains on residential property.You use AI every day.
