articles.title: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments
articles.summary: Perran Moon, MP for Camborne and Redruth, voluntarily referred himself for investigation.
articles.body:
A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation.

Moon, the MP for Camborne and Redruth, is listed on Companies House as the co-director of a training company called Autoswot , which last filed accounts in June 2021.

Government Bounce Back Loans of up to £50,000 were made available to support small businesses during the pandemic, but a government report found the scheme was vulnerable to fraud and error.

In August, Labour MP Bayo Alaba was suspended after queries about a Covid-era loan, and a third MP, James McMurdock, quit Reform in 2025 after questions about eligibility for loans he received.

Bounce back loans worth a total of £46bn were issued when the scheme was launched in May 2020, making it the biggest of the government's pandemic-era loan schemes.

Each one had a 100% government guarantee, meaning taxpayers' cash was used to pay back banks if the companies failed, but the Covid counter-fraud commissioner later found total fraud and error estimated at up to £2.8bn to the public purse.

Autoswot had been set up in June 2019, a year before the loans became available, and at that time had forecast revenues of more than £200,000.

Moon stressed he had applied for the maximum loan of £50,000 within the rules, regularly seeking professional advice about its obligations, and would provide documents to the Labour Party investigation into the matter.

He said the loan was used to pay for "staffing and other essential business costs" during the pandemic and partial repayments were made until the company ceased trading in late 2022.

The BBC understands that Moon was repeatedly assured in writing by Companies House that no accounts needed to be filed after the company applied to be struck off, but that guidance was incorrect.

Moon, who was first elected in the 2024 Labour landslide following a career in communications and marketing, said the business folded due to unforeseen external market pressures and "despite the best efforts of staff".

He said: "In order for these matters to be looked into, I have voluntarily referred myself to the Labour Party's investigations process and will cooperate fully with this process.

"The loan application was made in good faith, and the information provided, including the company's turnover forecast, was accurate and properly based.

"I will continue to work hard every day representing my constituents while this party process is ongoing."

A Labour Party spokesperson confirmed Moon had referred himself for investigation.

"The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and we have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld," they said.

"We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing."

This is the second investigation the Labour Party has launched into the loans, with Alaba, the MP for Southend East and Rochford , also referring himself for investigation over loans made to a real estate company, Alaba Properties.

At the time, Alaba said: "There has been no attempt to avoid my financial obligations, and I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full."

McMurdock, who now sits as an independent, was the first MP to be questioned over bounce back loans given to two fitness companies worth £70,000.

In 2025 McMurdock said all his business dealings had been compliant with the rules, adding that after taking "specialist legal advice" he had decided "to continue my parliamentary career as an independent MP".

articles.title: Jessica Alba turned a pregnancy concern into The Honest Company; its valuation reached nearly $2.1 billion after its first trading day
articles.summary: Jessica Alba was pregnant with her daughter Honor in 2008 when an experience involving a baby laundry detergent prompted her to question the ingredients
articles.body: Jessica Alba was pregnant with her daughter Honor in 2008 when an experience involving a baby laundry detergent prompted her to question the ingredients in everyday household products. Her search for alternatives helped inspire The Honest Company, a consumer-products business that launched in 2012 with 17 products for babies, personal care and the home. More than 9 years later, the company began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker HNST on May 5, 2021. Shares were priced at $16 in the initial public offering and rose 44% on their first day of trading, giving the company a market value of approximately $2.1 billion, according to the Associated Press. Its path from a founder’s concern to a publicly traded consumer brand illustrates how personal experience can inspire a business, while also showing the importance of substantiating the product claims on which a company’s reputation depends.Jessica Alba’s Honest Company origin story and the rise of baby-care productsAlba has described how her experience during pregnancy led her to examine product labels and look more closely at the ingredients in household and baby-care products. She approached Christopher Gavigan, author of Healthy Child Healthy World, and went on to build the business with Gavigan, Brian Lee and Sean Kane. The Honest Company launched in 2012 with 17 products, including diapers, wipes, personal-care items and household cleaners. It initially sold products directly to consumers through its website, including a subscription model designed to make recurring purchases easier for parents.The business expanded beyond its original online model as it developed a broader retail presence. Its product portfolio eventually covered three main categories: diapers and wipes, skin and personal care, and household and wellness. According to the company’s 2021 IPO filing, revenue increased by 28% in 2020 to approximately $300.5 million. The business nevertheless recorded a loss, underscoring the difference between revenue growth and profitability. Diapers and wipes accounted for 63% of revenue in 2020. The company also reported that, according to a third-party study it commissioned that year, nearly 90% of surveyed diaper buyers had expanded their purchases beyond diapers, while nearly half had purchased at least 2 other products from its portfolio. The findings suggested that diapers could introduce customers to other categories, including personal-care products and household cleaners. The statistic, however, describes surveyed buyers and should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every diaper customer would purchase additional products.Pregnancy, chemical exposure and the appeal of ingredient transparencyAlba’s concerns emerged in a wider conversation about the chemicals people encounter in everyday life. Scientific research has documented exposure to multiple environmental chemicals among pregnant women, although detecting a chemical in the body does not, on its own, establish that it caused harm or identify the product responsible. The Honest Company built its brand around ingredient transparency, product design and a focus on family and household needs. Alba’s public profile helped bring attention to that positioning, but the broader market context matters too: consumers differ in their priorities, and claims about safety or product performance need evidence specific to the products concerned.The Honest Company IPO: HNST shares, valuation and financial detailsThe company’s 2021 stock-market debut marked a major milestone. According to Renaissance Capital’s IPO report, The Honest Company priced its offering at $16 per share, within its indicated range of $14 to $17. The offering comprised 25.8 million shares at $16 each, representing approximately $413 million in gross offering value. However, that entire amount did not go to the company.
